BREAKING: Judge Kathaleen McCormick has agreed to step aside and reassign multiple high-profile lawsuits involving Elon Musk and his companies—including Tesla—to other Vice Chancellors in the Court of Chancery.

This follows a recent filing from Musk’s legal team flagging what they saw as clear bias: a screenshot showing her account “supporting” a LinkedIn post that openly celebrated a $2 billion verdict against him in a separate California fraud case. McCormick firmly denies any actual endorsement or bias (she even points out she dismissed a lawsuit against Musk just last year), but she’s handing the cases off anyway—citing the intense media scrutiny as harmful to the fair administration of justice.

For reference, this is the same judge who previously struck down Elon’s $56 billion Tesla pay package and presided over the Twitter-related litigation.

Here’s her full statement released today:

"Dear Counsel:

This letter addresses the motions for my recusal and to randomly reassign two of the three above-referenced actions.

The motion for recusal rests on a false premise—that I support a LinkedIn post about Mr. Musk, which I do not in fact support. I am not biased against the defendants in these actions. In fact, I dismissed a suit against Mr. Musk just last year. The motion for recusal is denied.

But the motion for reassignment is granted—I will reassign each of the three above-referenced actions. As should be obvious, disproportionate media attention surrounding a judge’s handling of an action is detrimental to the administration of justice. Fortunately, the Court of Chancery is far greater than any one person. I have complete faith in the Vice Chancellors’ abilities to adjudicate these matters. And three of them will.

Please contact my Chambers to obtain a time for the random reassignment. All counsel are welcome to attend. But each of the individuals who signed the motion for reassignment or the joinder in that motion must appear to witness what they requested."

🇯🇵 Japan’s demographic crisis deepens: The birth rate has been plummeting for decades, with continued decline in recent years.

Number of live births (approx.):
• 2018: ~919,000
• 2019: ~865,000
• 2020: ~841,000
• 2021: ~811,000
• 2022: ~771,000
• 2023: ~727,000
• 2024: ~686,000 (Japanese nationals)
• 2025: 705,809 (preliminary, including foreign nationals — new record low, 10th straight year of decline)

Total Fertility Rate (children per woman): Fell from ~1.42 in 2018 to a record low of 1.15 in 2024 — far below the 2.1 replacement level (2025 TFR data expected in June).

This is the lowest number of births since records began in 1899, accelerating population aging and straining pensions/healthcare.

Successive governments have tried incentives like child allowances, expanded childcare, and parental leave, but the trend continues. 😔
